subject: Copywriting
title: Framing: Same Fact, Different Feeling
description: A 60-second lesson on Framing: Same Fact, Different Feeling.

hook.text: '95% fat-free' outsells '5% fat.' Same yogurt, different frame. How you say it changes what people hear.

buildup.text: Tversky and Kahneman showed doctors chose differently based on framing. '90% survive' beat '10% die.' Same math.

discovery.text: Copy frames every claim. 'Save $50' vs 'Don't waste $50.' Gain frame vs loss frame—both true, different impact.

twist.text: Negative frames work better for prevention products. Positive frames work better for aspirational purchases.

climax.text: A skilled copywriter doesn't lie—they choose which truth to emphasize. Framing is selection, not deception.

punchline.text: Same fact, different words. Framing changes everything.

details.summary: Framing is the art of presenting the same information in different ways to change how people perceive it. '90% fat-free' and '10% fat' are identical facts, but the first feels healthy and the second sounds unhealthy. How you frame the truth matters as much as the truth itself.
details.whyItMatters: Every piece of copy involves framing choices. Understanding how framing shapes perception helps writers present truthful information in the most persuasive way — and helps readers see through frames that distort reality.
takeaways: Positive framing emphasizes gains; negative framing emphasizes losses
Loss frames are more motivating for risk-averse decisions
The same fact can feel completely different depending on its frame

faq.question: What is the difference between positive and negative framing?
faq.answer: 'This surgery has a 90% survival rate' (positive frame) versus 'this surgery has a 10% death rate' (negative frame). Same fact, completely different emotional impact. Positive framing emphasizes what you gain; negative framing emphasizes what you might lose.

faq.question: When should copywriters use loss framing versus gain framing?
faq.answer: Use gain framing for aspirational products — 'achieve more, feel better.' Use loss framing for protective products — 'don't miss out, avoid this risk.' Research shows loss framing is more effective when the stakes are high and the audience is risk-averse.
